{background-color="#1B3A6B"} # Brief recap 📚 {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Module 06: getting data from the web ### Lectures 18 and 19 :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 24px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - A web API is a [contract]{.alert} between your code and a server - We built URLs, read status codes and followed [JSON]{.alert} paths - `curl` and `requests` fetched the data - A `for` loop turned the reply into a DataFrame - A saved [snapshot]{.alert} gives the same numbers every time ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - Module 07: what if the data get [really big]{.alert}? - Three possible fixes: - [Parallel code]{.alert}: several cores at once - A [better algorithm]{.alert} - A [faster engine]{.alert}, like DuckDB (next lecture) :::{style="background: rgba(27, 58, 107, 0.08); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 20px; margin-top: 20px;"} Lecture 19's `wdi_panel.parquet` uses the parquet format we meet today ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Tweet of the day :::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: 50px; font-size: 22px;"} [![](figures/huang-tweet.png){width="75%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/huang-tweet.png"} [About Jensen Huang](https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/nvidia-ceo-jensen-huang-investigation-rcna608148) :::{style="font-size: 18px;"} Source: [X](https://x.com/FangYi11101/status/2119586357853204813) ::: ::: # Today's agenda {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Lecture outline :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - [Serial and parallel]{.alert} code, and the `map` function - [`joblib`]{.alert} and [`concurrent.futures`]{.alert}: parallel work on your laptop - [Big O notation]{.alert}: what parallelism can and cannot fix - [Amdahl's law]{.alert}: the limit on speed-up - [Dask]{.alert} for data bigger than your memory - Lazy arrays and DataFrames - CSV and parquet files - `dask.delayed` for your own functions - [Best practices]{.alert}: when to parallelise, and when not to ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: -30px;"} [![](figures/cores.webp){width="80%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/cores.webp"} [![](figures/dask.png){width="55%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/dask.png"} ::: ::: ::: ::: # Serial vs parallel algorithms {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Serial execution and the `map` function :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - Python runs one line after another - This loop calls `bar` on each number, one at a time: :::{style="font-size: 1.1em;"} ::: {#6facf592 .cell cache='true' execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np # An array of six numbers foo = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]) # A function that squares a number def bar(x): return x * x # Call bar on each element, in order for element in foo: print(bar(element)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0 1 4 9 16 25 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - [`map`]{.alert} applies one function to every element of a list - My own version shows the loop inside: :::{style="font-size: 1.1em;"} ::: {#02ac16c3 .cell cache='true' execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} def my_map(function, array): output = [] # empty list for the results for element in array: output.append(function(element)) return output my_map(bar, foo) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [np.int64(0), np.int64(1), np.int64(4), np.int64(9), np.int64(16), np.int64(25)] ``` ::: ::: ::: - Python has a [built-in](https://www.w3schools.com/python/ref_func_map.asp) `map` (faster than mine): :::{style="font-size: 1.1em;"} ::: {#a7ce355a .cell cache='true' execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} list(map(bar, foo)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` [np.int64(0), np.int64(1), np.int64(4), np.int64(9), np.int64(16), np.int64(25)] ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Using `joblib` for parallel computing :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 20px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - Each call to `bar` is [independent]{.alert}, so the calls can run at once - Your CPU has several [cores]{.alert}. Each runs one task at a time - [`joblib`](https://joblib.readthedocs.io/) sends tasks to [worker processes]{.alert}: separate copies of Python - `Parallel(n_jobs=6)` runs up to six tasks at once. `n_jobs=-1` uses all cores - `delayed(bar)` wraps `bar`, so a worker runs it later - `delayed(bar)(x) for x in foo` is a [generator expression](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/python/generator-expressions/): a `for` loop inside parentheses that makes one task per element - More information about joblib on their website: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - With `bar` and `foo` from before: :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#2e1a974c .cell cache='true' execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Install joblib if you haven't done so yet # !pip install joblib from joblib import Parallel, delayed results = Parallel(n_jobs=6)( delayed(bar)(x) for x in foo ) results ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` [np.int64(0), np.int64(1), np.int64(4), np.int64(9), np.int64(16), np.int64(25)] ``` ::: ::: ::: - Each worker gets a different element of `foo` - The results match the serial version ::: ::: ::: ## Serial vs parallel execution :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 20px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - Our function `calculation` (below) runs ten heavy steps on ten million random numbers - The calls are independent, so the problem is [embarrassingly parallel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embarrassingly_parallel) - [`%timeit`](https://ipython.readthedocs.io/en/stable/interactive/magics.html#magic-timeit) averages a line over several runs (Jupyter only) - `%%timeit` (two `%` signs) times a whole cell - [One call:]{.alert} :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#0840aeb4 .cell cache='true' execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} def calculation(size=10000000): # Create a large array and perform operations arr = np.random.rand(size) for _ in range(10): arr = np.sqrt(arr) + np.sin(arr) return np.mean(arr) # Single run %timeit calculation() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 333 ms ± 5.25 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - [Four calls, one after another:]{.alert} - `_` names a loop variable we do not use :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#b237b397 .cell cache='true' execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Sequential runs (4 times) %timeit [calculation() for _ in range(4)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1.34 s ± 8.59 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each) ``` ::: ::: ::: - [Four calls, in parallel:]{.alert} :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#dd8717fe .cell cache='true' execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} %%timeit # Parallel runs (4 times) Parallel(n_jobs=4)( delayed(calculation)() for _ in range(4) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 471 ms ± 4.6 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each) ``` ::: ::: ::: - Not a full 4× speed-up, because [starting workers and collecting results takes time]{.alert} ::: ::: ::: # concurrent.futures {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## `concurrent.futures`: the standard-library option :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 21px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - [`concurrent.futures`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html) comes with Python: nothing to install - [Computing]{.alert} (maths, model training): [`ProcessPoolExecutor`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html#concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor) - [Waiting]{.alert} (downloads, API calls): [`ThreadPoolExecutor`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html#concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor) - Processes are separate copies of Python that compute at the same time - Threads share one copy of Python, so they start fast. While one waits, the others keep working :::{style="font-size: 1.1em;"} ::: {#59cc7c7f .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as executor: results = list(executor.map(bar, foo)) ``` ::: ::: - In a notebook, [import `bar` from a `.py` file]{.alert}. Workers cannot see functions defined in a cell, but joblib can ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - Threads start fast and need no extra core to wait - Each URL asks the [World Bank API](https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/898581-api-basic-call-structures) for one country's population :::{style="font-size: 1.1em;"} ::: {#a73d83d8 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor import requests base = "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/" end = "/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL?format=json&per_page=100" urls = [base + "BRA" + end, base + "IND" + end, base + "USA" + end] def fetch(url): return requests.get(url, timeout=30).json() with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as executor: results = list(executor.map(fetch, urls)) ``` ::: ::: - All three requests wait at once (Lecture 19 sent one at a time) ::: ::: ::: ## When to use which? :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - [joblib](https://joblib.readthedocs.io/) suits numeric loops, and [scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/) uses it when you set `n_jobs=-1` - [`load_digits()`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.datasets.load_digits.html) loads 1,797 small images of handwritten digits - 6 combinations × 3 folds (`cv=3`) = 18 fits shared across the cores :::{style="font-size: 1.1em;"} ::: {#ab62ef41 .cell cache='true' execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.datasets import load_digits from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV from sklearn.svm import SVC import time digits = load_digits() param_grid = {"C": [0.1, 1, 10], "gamma": [0.001, 0.01]} start = time.time() search = GridSearchCV(SVC(), param_grid, cv=3, n_jobs=-1) search.fit(digits.data, digits.target) elapsed = time.time() - start print(f"Best score: {search.best_score_:.3f}") print(f"Time: {elapsed:.2f}s (all cores)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Best score: 0.976 Time: 1.97s (all cores) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="margin-top: 30px; margin-bottom: 30px;"} | Scenario | Tool | |----------|------| | sklearn / numeric loops | `joblib` (`n_jobs=-1`) | | Download many files | `ThreadPoolExecutor` | | CPU-heavy, no dependencies | `ProcessPoolExecutor` | | Bigger than RAM, clusters | `Dask` (next section) | ::: :::{style="background: rgba(27, 58, 107, 0.08); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 20px; margin-top: 20px;"} Every tool [splits the work, runs it on separate workers, then collects the results]{.alert} ::: ::: ::: ::: # Big O notation {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Big O notation :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 24px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - [Big O notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_O_notation) describes how runtime grows with input size - [O(1)]{.alert} is constant: reading one array element takes the same time at any size - A single loop is [O(n)]{.alert}, linear: double the input, double the time - A nested loop is [O(n²)]{.alert}, quadratic: double the input, four times the time - Calling `calculation` `n` times is [O(n)]{.alert}: 100 calls take 100 times as long as one ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{.plot-first style="text-align: center;"} ::: {#84b8ef77 .cell cache='true' execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np # Simulate processing times num_images = np.array([1, 10, 50, 100, 200]) sequential_time = num_images * 2 # 2 seconds per image parallel_time = (num_images * 2) / 4 # 4 cores, ideal speedup plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5)) plt.plot(num_images, sequential_time, 'o-', label='Serial O(n)', linewidth=2, markersize=8) plt.plot(num_images, parallel_time, 's-', label='Parallel on 4 cores (still O(n))', linewidth=2, markersize=8) plt.xlabel('Number of Images', fontsize=12) plt.ylabel('Time (seconds)', fontsize=12) plt.title('O(n) Scaling: Serial vs Parallel', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold') plt.legend(fontsize=11) plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](21-parallel-computing_files/figure-revealjs/cell-12-output-1.png){width=670 height=454} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## What parallelism does to complexity :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 20px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - With `p` cores, an O(n) task takes about [n/p time plus overhead]{.alert}. It is still O(n) - Best candidates: [embarrassingly parallel O(n) tasks]{.alert}, which share no data and do not wait for each other :::{style="background: rgba(230, 57, 70, 0.1); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 20px; margin-top: 20px;"} Parallelism divides the time by a constant but never changes the Big O class. [O(n²) on eight cores is still O(n²)]{.alert} ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - Parallelism cannot fix this: :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#85259e41 .cell cache='true' execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} # O(n^2): every pair of elements def pairwise_sum(data): n = len(data) results = [] for i in range(n): for j in range(n): results.append(data[i] + data[j]) return results data = list(range(1_000)) print(f"{len(pairwise_sum(data)):,} operations") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1,000,000 operations ``` ::: ::: ::: - 1,000 elements give 1 million operations - `n = 100_000` gives 10 billion. Eight cores still leave 1.25 billion each - Poor candidates for parallelism: - Steps that need results from a previous step - Tasks that share the same data - Tasks limited by memory, not by the CPU ::: ::: ::: ## Try it yourself! {#sec:exercise01} :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 20px;"} 1. Run `pip install joblib numpy` if you have not already 2. Run the serial version below and write down the time it prints. `np.arange(1000000)` makes an array of the numbers 0 to 999,999 :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#d556fe65 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np def square(x): return x**2 # Create a large array to process numbers = np.arange(1000000) # Sequential version %timeit [square(x) for x in numbers] ``` ::: ::: 3. Run the parallel version and write down its time. It takes a few seconds :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#a53586c5 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} from joblib import Parallel, delayed # Parallel version %timeit Parallel(n_jobs=4)(delayed(square)(x) for x in numbers) ``` ::: ::: 4. Compare the two times and decide which version you would use [[Appendix 01]{.button}](#sec:appendix01) ::: # Amdahl's law {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Amdahl's law: the speed-up ceiling :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 24px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - Some parts of a program [cannot run in parallel]{.alert}: setup, merging results, or steps that wait for the one before - That part is the [serial share]{.alert} $s$. The rest, $p = 1 - s$, can be split across cores - More cores only speed up $p$, so $s$ sets a ceiling ([Amdahl's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amdahl%27s_law)) - $\text{speedup} = \dfrac{1}{s + \dfrac{p}{N}}$, with $N$ = cores - Example: 90% parallel ($s = 0.1$) on 8 cores gives $\frac{1}{0.1 + 0.9/8} = \frac{1}{0.2125} \approx 4.7\times$, not $8\times$ - With infinite cores, the limit is $1/0.1 = 10\times$ ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{.plot-first style="text-align: center;"} ::: {#8a816cfe .cell cache='true' execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np cores = np.arange(1, 65) serial_fracs = [0.05, 0.2, 0.5] labels = ["95% parallel", "80% parallel", "50% parallel"] colours = ["#1B3A6B", "#E07A24", "#2CA02C"] plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5)) for s, lab, c in zip(serial_fracs, labels, colours): speedup = 1 / (s + (1 - s) / cores) plt.plot(cores, speedup, label=lab, linewidth=2, color=c) plt.xlabel("Number of cores", fontsize=12) plt.ylabel("Speed-up (×)", fontsize=12) plt.title("Amdahl's law: speed-up vs core count", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold") plt.legend(fontsize=11) plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](21-parallel-computing_files/figure-revealjs/cell-16-output-1.png){width=759 height=469} ::: ::: ::: :::{style="background: rgba(27, 58, 107, 0.08); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 20px; margin-top: 15px;"} Ten people chop vegetables faster than one, but the oven still takes 10 minutes. Dinner can never be faster than the oven ::: ::: ::: ::: # Dask {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Dask :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="52%"} - [Dask](https://dask.org/) is a Python library for parallel computing - It handles [data bigger than your RAM](https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/best-practices.html) and runs on [clusters](https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/deploying.html) of many machines - You write [NumPy](https://numpy.org/) or [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org/) code, and Dask runs it in parallel - A [task scheduler](https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/scheduling.html) splits the work into small tasks and spreads them over your cores - Dask offers [arrays](https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/array.html), [DataFrames](https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/dataframe.html) and [bags](https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/bag.html) (parallel lists) - Latest release: [2026.8.0](https://github.com/dask/dask/releases/tag/2026.8.0) (August 2026) - Next lecture times the same group-by in [DuckDB](https://duckdb.org/), pandas and Dask ::: :::{.column width="48%"} :::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: -10px;"} [![](figures/dask-homepage-2026.png){width="88%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/dask-homepage-2026.png"} :::{style="font-size: 17px;"} ::: :::{style="background: rgba(27, 58, 107, 0.08); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 20px; margin-top: 15px; text-align: left;"} `joblib` splits the work into function calls. [Dask also splits the data into chunks]{.alert}, so the data can be bigger than your RAM ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Dask arrays :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 20px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#ebe944ca .cell cache='true' execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} import dask.dataframe as dd import dask.array as da ``` ::: ::: - A [Dask array](https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/array.html) splits a large array into [chunks]{.alert} - Each chunk is a [NumPy array](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.ndarray.html), processed in parallel - Here each chunk is 100 by 100: :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#1665ab77 .cell cache='true' execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} data = np.random.normal(size=100000).reshape(200, 500) a = da.from_array(data, chunks=(100, 100)) a ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ```{=html}
Array Chunk
Bytes 781.25 kiB 78.12 kiB
Shape (200, 500) (100, 100)
Dask graph 10 chunks in 1 graph layer
Data type float64 numpy.ndarray
``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - Dask arrays are [lazy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lazy_evaluation): Dask plans the steps first, which [saves memory]{.alert} - Slicing gives a plan, not numbers: :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#b0ab1bc7 .cell cache='true' execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} a[:10, 5] # first 10 rows of the 6th column ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ```{=html}
Array Chunk
Bytes 80 B 80 B
Shape (10,) (10,)
Dask graph 1 chunks in 2 graph layers
Data type float64 numpy.ndarray
``` ::: ::: ::: - `.compute()` [runs the plan]{.alert}: :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#f8384b1f .cell cache='true' execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} a[:10, 5].compute() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ``` array([-1.22254226, -0.20602161, -1.73760655, -0.47669143, 0.73397732, 0.79288256, 0.36582556, -0.61382531, -0.66821034, -0.26960348]) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Dask arrays :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 21px;"} - Maths (`+`, `*`, `exp`, `log`) and summaries (`sum()`, `mean()`, `std()`) work as in NumPy ([full list](https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/array-numpy-compatibility.html)) :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#fa9cae1a .cell cache='true' execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} a.sum().compute() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ``` np.float64(-205.97997407969373) ``` ::: ::: ::: - `sqrt` plus `sin` on 100 million numbers, first in NumPy: :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#3a887eb6 .cell cache='true' execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} size = 100000000 np_arr = np.random.random(size) %timeit np_result = np.sqrt(np_arr) + np.sin(np_arr) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 395 ms ± 3.56 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each) ``` ::: ::: ::: - Then in Dask, with automatic chunks: :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#3edff5f4 .cell cache='true' execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} da_arr = da.random.random(size, chunks='auto') %timeit (da.sqrt(da_arr) + da.sin(da_arr)).compute() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 239 ms ± 8.23 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each) ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{style="background: rgba(230, 57, 70, 0.1); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 20px; margin-top: 15px;"} NumPy uses one core here and Dask uses several. On small data, Dask is often [slower]{.alert} ::: ::: ## Dask dataframes :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - A [Dask DataFrame](https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/dataframe.html) is many small [pandas DataFrames](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html), [split by row](https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/dataframe-design.html) - [`dask.datasets.timeseries()`](https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/api.html#dask.datasets.timeseries) makes random example data: one row per second from 1 to 30 January 2000 :::{style="font-size: 1.2em; margin-top: 20px; margin-bottom: 20px;"} ::: {#14c85c49 .cell cache='true' execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} import dask df = dask.datasets.timeseries() ``` ::: ::: - Computed, it would take about 120 MB of memory - Dask DataFrames are [lazy](https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/graphs.html), like Dask arrays - The table shows `...`, because no rows have been computed yet ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="font-size: 22px;"} ::: {#6edf5258 .cell cache='true' execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} df ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ```{=html}

Parquet loads 30 days but [only the 2 columns we named]{.alert} :::{style="background: rgba(230, 57, 70, 0.1); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 20px; margin-top: 15px;"} Use parquet for files over 100 MB, or with [many columns]{.alert} when you need only a few. Keep [CSV]{.alert} for small files and anything a colleague will open in Excel ::: ::: ::: ::: # Dask delayed {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Dask delayed :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - [`dask.delayed`](https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/delayed.html) parallelises functions you already have - No Dask DataFrame or array needed - First, four calls in a row: :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#5f7eeffe .cell cache='true' execution_count=41} ``` {.python .cell-code} def calculation(size=10000000): arr = np.random.rand(size) for _ in range(10): arr = np.sqrt(arr) + np.sin(arr) return np.mean(arr) %timeit [calculation() for _ in range(4)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1.37 s ± 46.6 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - A [decorator](https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-decorator) is an `@` line above a `def`. It changes what the function does - With `@dask.delayed`, calling the function creates a task instead of running it :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#7a5bac15 .cell cache='true' execution_count=42} ``` {.python .cell-code} @dask.delayed def delayed_calculation(size=10000000): arr = np.random.rand(size) for _ in range(10): arr = np.sqrt(arr) + np.sin(arr) return np.mean(arr) results = [] for _ in range(4): results.append(delayed_calculation()) # Compute all results at once %timeit final_results = dask.compute(*results) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 510 ms ± 11 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each) ``` ::: ::: ::: - `dask.compute(*results)` runs all four tasks. `*` unpacks the list into four arguments ::: ::: ::: ## Dask delayed :::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 21px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="55%"} - Three functions on three input sizes: nine tasks in three branches :::{style="font-size: 1.1em;"} ::: {#d1f7e06d .cell cache='true' execution_count=43} ``` {.python .cell-code} @dask.delayed def generate_data(size): return np.random.rand(size) @dask.delayed def transform_data(data): return np.sqrt(data) + np.sin(data) @dask.delayed def aggregate_data(data): return np.mean(data) # Build the tasks (nothing runs yet) dask_results = [] for size in [1_000_000, 2_000_000, 3_000_000]: data = generate_data(size) transformed = transform_data(data) dask_results.append(aggregate_data(transformed)) %timeit dask.compute(*dask_results) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 23.1 ms ± 636 μs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="45%"} - `dask.visualize()` draws the plan without running it :::{.taskgraph style="font-size: 1.2em; text-align: center;"} ::: {#1863a8ac .cell cache='true' execution_count=44} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Needs graphviz: pip install graphviz # plus brew/apt install graphviz dask.visualize(*dask_results) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=39} ![](21-parallel-computing_files/figure-revealjs/cell-44-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: :::{style="background: rgba(27, 58, 107, 0.08); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 20px; margin-top: 10px;"} Dask sees all nine tasks first. The branches are independent, so they can run on separate workers ::: ::: ::: ::: ## The Dask dashboard :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="52%"} - `from dask.distributed import Client`, then `client = Client()`, opens a dashboard at `localhost:8787` - Install it first: `pip install "dask[distributed]" bokeh` - The picture shows our three-step pipeline, run in a loop - Each row is one worker thread, and each coloured bar is one task - Purple is `generate_data`, teal is `transform_data`, and green is `aggregate_data` - Bars stacked on top of each other ran at the same time - Use it to check that your work runs in parallel ::: :::{.column width="48%"} :::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: -10px;"} [![](figures/dask-dashboard-task-stream-2026.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/dask-dashboard-task-stream-2026.png"} :::{style="font-size: 17px;"} Dashboard at `localhost:8787`, running on my laptop ::: :::{style="background: rgba(27, 58, 107, 0.08); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 20px; margin-top: 15px;"} White space means an idle thread. Big gaps usually mean the chunks are too big, so there are fewer tasks than threads ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: # Best practices {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Best practices :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - [Measure first]{.alert} with `%timeit`. Amdahl's law says what fixing the slow part is worth - Check that tasks are [independent]{.alert} and big enough to be worth a worker - A [better algorithm]{.alert} often beats parallel code on large inputs - A [faster engine]{.alert} like DuckDB may beat parallel pandas (next lecture) - NumPy or pandas may already have a fast [built-in]{.alert} function - Do you need all the data? Try a [sample]{.alert} first ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - Our [parquet]{.alert} group-by was about 10× faster than CSV - Call `.compute()` and `.persist()` [rarely]{.alert}: each call runs the whole plan - [Try a few chunk sizes]{.alert}, or start with `chunks='auto'` - More tips in the [Dask best practices](https://docs.dask.org/en/latest/best-practices.html) :::{style="background: rgba(230, 57, 70, 0.1); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 20px; margin-top: 15px;"} The [most common mistake]{.alert} is parallelising before measuring. More cores will not fix a slow disk or an $O(n^2)$ loop ::: ::: ::: ::: # Summary {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## What we learned today :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - [Serial and parallel code]{.alert}: `map`, embarrassingly parallel problems, `joblib` - [`concurrent.futures`]{.alert}: processes for CPU work, threads for waiting - [Big O notation]{.alert}: parallelism divides the time, but the growth rate stays the same - [Amdahl's law]{.alert}: the serial share caps the speed-up - [Dask]{.alert}: lazy arrays and DataFrames for data bigger than RAM - [`dask.delayed`]{.alert} parallelises your own functions, and `dask.visualize` shows the plan - [Parquet]{.alert}: our data shrank from 182 MB to 86 MB, and the group-by ran about 10× faster - [Best practices]{.alert}: measure before you parallelise ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - Next lecture, [SQL Revision with DuckDB]{.alert}: SQL on the WDI panel, and the same group-by in DuckDB, pandas and Dask :::{style="display: flex; justify-content: center; font-size: 24px; margin-top: 30px; margin-bottom: 30px;"} | Engine | Language | Parallel? | Bigger than RAM? | |--------|----------|-----------|-------------| | pandas | Python/C | Single-threaded | No | | Polars | Rust | All cores | Yes (streaming) | | DuckDB | C++ | All cores | Yes | | Dask | Python | All cores + clusters | Yes | ::: - Polars is covered in [tutorial 07](https://danilofreire.github.io/datasci350/07-polars-tutorial.html) - SQL on DataFrames before then: [tutorial 04](https://danilofreire.github.io/datasci350/04-duckdb-sql-tutorial.html) ::: ::: ::: # Thank you! 😊 {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Appendix 01 {#sec:appendix01} :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 24px;"} ::: {#1215d607 .cell cache='true' execution_count=45} ``` {.python .cell-code} def square(x): return x**2 # Create a large array to process numbers = np.arange(1000000) # Sequential version %timeit [square(x) for x in numbers] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 44.6 ms ± 604 μs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#7a5afcd2 .cell cache='true' execution_count=46} ``` {.python .cell-code} from joblib import Parallel, delayed # Parallel version %timeit Parallel(n_jobs=4)(delayed(square)(x) for x in numbers) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1.9 s ± 55.8 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each) ``` ::: ::: - The parallel version is [slower]{.alert} here - `square(x)` is so fast that sending a million tiny tasks to the workers costs more than the work - Parallel computing pays off when each task is heavy [[Back to exercise]{.button}](#sec:exercise01) ::: ## Appendix 02 {#sec:appendix02} :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 22px;"} - Ten million random numbers, computing `mean(sqrt(x^2))` at four chunk sizes - Medium chunks (2 million) win on my laptop ::: {#654a51fe .cell cache='true' execution_count=47} ``` {.python .cell-code} size = 10_000_000 # Dask with SMALL chunks # 100 chunks da_data_small = da.random.random(size, chunks=100_000) %timeit da.sqrt(da_data_small**2).mean().compute() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 39.5 ms ± 800 μs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#31b80f97 .cell cache='true' execution_count=48} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Dask with MEDIUM chunks # 5 chunks da_data_medium = da.random.random(size, chunks=2_000_000) %timeit da.sqrt(da_data_medium**2).mean().compute() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 13.6 ms ± 179 μs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100 loops each) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#b7337caf .cell cache='true' execution_count=49} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Dask with LARGE chunks # 2 chunks da_data_large = da.random.random(size, chunks=5_000_000) %timeit da.sqrt(da_data_large**2).mean().compute() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 20.4 ms ± 826 μs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#270ed35f .cell cache='true' execution_count=50} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Dask with AUTO chunks # Dask picks da_data_auto = da.random.random(size, chunks='auto') %timeit da.sqrt(da_data_auto**2).mean().compute() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 31.6 ms ± 379 μs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each) ``` ::: ::: [[Back to exercise]{.button}](#sec:exercise02) ::: ## Appendix 02: why medium chunks win :::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 24px;"} - Every chunk becomes a few tasks, and each task has a [fixed overhead]{.alert}: Dask plans it, sends it to a worker and collects the result - [Small chunks]{.alert} (100): hundreds of tiny tasks, so most of the time goes on overhead - [Large chunks]{.alert} (2): little overhead, but only 2 cores have work - [Medium chunks]{.alert} (5): 5 cores busy, few tasks to manage - [Auto]{.alert} aims for about 128 MB per chunk. Our 80 MB array becomes one chunk on one core - Best size: big enough that overhead is small, small enough that every core gets work - My laptop has 10 cores, so about 10-20 chunks would probably be faster still [[Back to exercise]{.button}](#sec:exercise02) :::
